<reflection>
- The first experiment successfully separated the models into two main tiers. The top tier (M6, M8, M7, M3) has NLL around -23.5, while the standard Michaelis-Menten (M1) and others are around -18.1.
- The top models all introduce a mechanism that can cause an initial delay or non-linear rate dependence (an induction period). M6 and M8 involve unimolecular catalyst activation. M3 involves bimolecular catalyst dimerization. M7 involves a second substrate binding step.
- My aim was achieved as we have a clear set of leading hypotheses that share a specific kinetic feature that standard models cannot capture.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To distinguish between unimolecular activation (M6/M8), bimolecular dimerization (M3), and substrate-assisted catalysis (M7), we need to decouple the effects of [cat] and [S] on the reaction's acceleration phase. 
By significantly lowering the catalyst concentration (from 0.1 to 0.02) and increasing the substrate concentration (from 1.0 to 3.0), we can observe how the induction period and overall rate change.
- If M6 or M8 is correct, the unimolecular activation rate (`cat => cat*`) is independent of [cat]. Thus, the induction time will remain unchanged compared to the first experiment, even though the overall rate will drop linearly with [cat].
- If M3 is correct, the bimolecular dimerization (`2cat <=> cat2`) depends strongly on [cat]. Lowering [cat] by a factor of 5 will drastically increase the induction time and reduce the rate quadratically (by a factor of 25).
- If M7 is correct, increasing [S] will accelerate the formation of the active `catS2` complex, reducing any apparent induction delay and significantly boosting the rate relative to linear scaling.
This single experiment will cleanly separate the top 4 mechanisms by probing the reaction order of the activation phase.
</hypothesis>
